notes.text: Judah and his brethren were waiting for an answer, and could not but be amazed to discover, instead of the gravity of a judge, the natural affection of a father or brother. Cause every man to go out — The private conversations of friends are the most free. When Joseph would put on love, he puts off state, which it was not fit his servants should be witnesses of. Thus Christ graciously manifests himself and his loving kindness to his people, out of the sight and hearing of the world. See note at "ver. 2" for continuation to item

Tears were the introduction to his discourse. He had dammed up this stream a great while, and with much ado, but now it swelled so high that he could no longer contain, but he wept aloud, so that those whom he had forbid to see him could not but hear him. These were tears of tenderness and strong affection, and with these he threw off that austerity, with which he had hitherto carried himself towards his brethren; for he could bear it no longer. This represents the Divine compassion towards returning penitents, as much as that of the father of the prodigal, Luke xv, 20 Hosea xi, 8, 9. See note at "ver. 3" for continuation to item No. 3

He abruptly tells them; I am Joseph — They knew him only by his Egyptian name, Zaphnath-paaneah, his Hebrew name being lost and forgot in Egypt; but now he teaches them to call him by that, I am Joseph: nay, that they might not suspect it was another of the same name, he explains himself. I am Joseph your brother. This would both humble them yet more for their sin in selling him, and encourage them to hope for kind treatment. This word, at first, startled Joseph's brethren, they started back through fear, or at least stood still astonished: but Joseph called kindly and familiarly to them. Come near, I pray you. Thus, when Christ manifests himself to his people he encourages them to draw near to him with a true heart. Perhaps being about to speak of their selling of him, he would not speak aloud, lest the Egyptians should overhear, and it should make the Hebrews to be yet more an abomination to them; therefore he would have them come near, that he might whisper with them, which, now the tide of his passion was a little over, he was able to do, whereas, at first, he could not but cry out.

He endeavours to sweep their grief for the injuries they had done him, by shewing them, that, whatever they designed, God meant it for good, and had brought much good out of it. See note at "ver. 1" for start of item, ie. No. 1

Be not grieved or angry with yourselves — Sinners must grieve, and be angry with themselves for their sins; yea, though God, by his power, bring good out of them, for that is no thanks to the sinner: but true penitents should be greatly affected with it, when they see God bringing good out of evil. Though we must not with this consideration extenuate our own sins, and so take off the edge of our repentance; yet it may do well thus to extenuate the sins of others, and so take off the edge of our angry resentments. Thus Joseph doth here. His brethren needed not to fear that he would revenge upon them an injury which God's providence had made to turn so much to his advantage, and that of his family. Now he tells them how long the famine was likely to last, five years yet, ver. 6, and what a capacity he was in of being kind to his relations, which is the greatest satisfaction that wealth and power can give to a good man.

See what a favourable colour he puts upon the injury they had done him, God sent me before you — God's Israel is the particular care of God's providence. Joseph reckoned that his advancement was not so much designed to save a whole kingdom of Egyptians, as to preserve a small family of Israelites; for the Lord's portion is his people: whatever goes with others, they shall be secured. How admirable are the projects of Providence! How remote its tendencies! What wheels are there within wheels; and yet all directed by the eyes in the wheels, and the Spirit of the living Creature! See note at "ver. 1" for start of item, ie. No. [1.] [5.] He promises to take care of his father and all his family, during the rest of the years of famine. (1.) He desires that his father might speedily be made glad with the tidings of his life and honour. His brethren must hasten to Canaan, and acquaint Jacob that his son Joseph was Lord of all Egypt - He knew it would be a refreshing oil to his hoary head, and a sovereign cordial to his spirits. He desires them to give themselves, and take with them to their father, all possible satisfaction of the truth of these surprising tidings.

Your eyes see that it is my mouth — If they could recollect themselves, they might remember something of his features and speech, and be satisfied. See note at "ver. 1" for (2.) He is very earnest that his father and all his family should come to him to Egypt. Come down unto me, tarry not - He allots his dwelling in Goshen, that part of Egypt which lay towards Canaan, that they might be mindful of the country from which they were to come out. He promiseth to provide for him, I will nourish - Our Lord Jesus being, like Joseph, exalted to the highest honours and powers of the upper world, it is his will that all that are his should be with him where he is. This is his commandment, that we be with him now in faith and hope, and a heavenly conversation; and this is his promise, that we shall be forever with him.

glossa.text: « God sent me, » etc. ((AUG. Quaest. in Gen., tom. III.)) What is it that according to other copies is read thus: « For God sent me before you, that your remnant should remain upon the earth, and that he might nourish up a great seed of your remnant? » For this does not agree in every point, etc., *as far as* « and so all Israel should be saved. »

« Thou shalt dwell in the land of Gessen, » etc. ((HIERON.)) In the Hebrew there stands *Gosen* ( )Migne prints a Hebrew word within these parentheses; our digitized source has lost it and left them empty.. Whence the error grew up that the land of Gessen is in Arabia. Further, as it stands in our codices, it is written with a final *m*, Gessem, which by no means pleases me, as signifying a land rained upon. For Gessem is turned into *rain* , where also in very many copies Gessem is found.

notes.text: Ointment — It is no less grateful and refreshing than that oil which was poured forth upon Aaron's head at the time of his consecration to the priestly office. Skirts - Not to the lower skirt or bottom of his sacerdotal garment, but to the upper skirt of it, or the mouth of it, as the Hebrew word properly signifies.

Zion — It is as desirable as the dew which falls upon mount Hermon, nay, as desirable as that heavenly dew of God's ordinances and graces which he hath commanded to fall upon the mountains of Zion and Moriah, and others which are round about Jerusalem. There - Where brethren live in peace and unity. In this Psalm the priests or Levites who watched all night in the temple, exhort one another, and pray for one another, ver. 1-3. A song of degrees.

glossa.text: *A canticle of degrees.* ((ID.)) The fourteenth degree: charity, which makes brethren to dwell in one, whence blessing and life. *Behold how good.* And this psalm is an atom, etc., *as far as* here therefore the just man, rejoicing over the dwelling together of brethren, says: *Behold how. Behold how.* ((AUG.)) That verse, most famous in the whole world, has as the trumpet of the Holy Ghost gathered together them that were divided: it has brought forth very many monasteries. ((CASS.)) *Behold.* As though more were set forth by the showing than could be unfolded by the tongue. *To dwell in one.* ((AUG.)) This concerning all Christians, but it properly befits monasteries, from which nevertheless the blessing comes down to the rest, as also to those brethren of Judaea, of whom it is said: *They had one heart,* and *one soul.*

*As the ointment.* ((THEOD.)) The priestly oil, etc., *as far as* it perfects the odour of perfect virtue. *The beard.* ((AUG.)) Behold the determination, that is, upon the apostles and the other primitive saints, who first strove in faith, but could not be overcome, because they had already gone before the head that had suffered *praecesserunt*; read *praecesserat*, "the head had gone before". *Aaron.* The priest who offered up himself, etc., *as far as* but they could not be overcome. From them. *To the skirt.* ((CASS.)) Or by the *skirt,* which is the edge of the garment, etc., *as far as* the profit of concord reaches even to them that are subject.

*As the dew.* ((ID.)) *Dew* is thin water, whence the earth brings forth, and it signifies grace, whereby sinners are converted. *Hermon.* ((AUG.)) According to the letter a mountain beyond Jordan, etc., *as far as* the rest are taken up, who are *in one* in heart.

notes.text: Hath God rejected his whole people — All Israel? In no wise. Now there is "a remnant" who believe, ver. 5; and hereafter "all Israel will be saved," ver. 26.

God hath not rejected that part of his people whom he foreknew — Speaking after the manner of men. For, in fact, knowing and foreknowing are the same thing with God, who knows or sees all things at once, from everlasting to everlasting. Know ye not - That in a parallel case, amidst a general apostasy, when Elijah thought the whole nation was fallen into idolatry, God "knew" there was "a remnant" of true worshippers.
For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance — God does not repent of his gifts to the Jews, or his calling of the gentiles.

For God hath shut up all together in disobedience — Suffering each in their turn to revolt from him. First, God suffered the gentiles in the early age to revolt, and took the family of Abraham as a peculiar seed to himself. Afterwards he permitted them to fall through unbelief, and took in the believing gentiles. And he did even this to provoke the Jews to jealousy, and so bring them also in the end to faith. This was truly a mystery in the divine conduct, which the apostle adores with such holy astonishment.

glossa.text: *I say then.* Because he had confuted the Jews by so many authorities, the gentiles might insult them, saying that they had been wholly cast off.

*He foreknew.* For *he predestined* he has set *he foreknew*. For so it ought to be taken, as is plain from what follows; and he said *he foreknew* for this reason, lest the Jews should again be proud from that whereby he said that they were not cast off, and were the people of God.

((AUG.)) Or will anyone dare to say that God did not foreknow to whom he was to give that they should believe, or whom he was to give to his Son, that of them he should lose none? And if he foreknew these things, assuredly he foreknew his own benefits, by which he deigns to set us free. This predestination of the saints is nothing else than the foreknowledge, that is, and the preparation, of God's benefits, by which they are most certainly set free, whosoever are set free.

*Or know ye not.* As if he should say: so the Lord has not cast off the remnant in this time, but has saved them; just as in the time of Elias he reserved many to himself, when Elias seemed to himself to be alone; and if he was ignorant that others also besides himself were reserved, it is no wonder if these are ignorant.
*For as.* That is, by what reason God once permitted you not to believe, namely lest you should have cause of being proud after you were converted.
*That they also.* Having learned by experience that salvation is not through the law, but through grace: that so they also may obtain mercy through humility.

*He hath concluded.* That is, he permitted them to be concluded. Here he seems in some manner to expound the mystery. *For God hath concluded all things in the unbelieving,* that they, confounded by repenting of the bitterness of their unbelief, converted by believing to the sweetness of God's mercy, might remain the more humble, so that both the grace of the gift might be most welcome, and they might cry out: *How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord ((Psal. XXX.)) Of all.* That is, of the Jews and of the gentiles, not that he will damn none, which some have falsely supposed.

notes.text: Every plant — That is, every doctrine.
Let them alone — If they are indeed blind leaders of the blind; let them alone: concern not yourselves about them: a plain direction how to behave with regard to all such. Luke vi, 39.
Are ye also yet without understanding — How fair and candid are the sacred historians? Never concealing or excusing their own blemishes.
First evil thoughts — then murders - and the rest. Railings - The Greek word includes all reviling, backbiting, and evil speaking.
Mark vii, 24.

A woman of Canaan — Canaan was also called Syrophenicia, as lying between Syria properly so called, and Phenicia, by the sea side. Cried to him - From afar, Thou Son of David - So she had some knowledge of the promised Messiah.
He answered her not a word — He sometimes tries our faith in like manner.
I am not sent — Not primarily; not yet.
Then came she — Into the house where he now was.
Thy faith — Thy reliance on the power and goodness of God.

glossa.text: *Not that which entereth in.* There is nothing outside a man that defiles him within, nor meat offered to idols in this, that it is God's creature; by one word every superstition of observances is struck down, when religion is thought to lie in distinguishing foods.

*Then the disciples, drawing near.* Great is the Pharisees' religion in the matter of foods, who on hearing this word were scandalized, that is, were indignant. *They were scandalized.* Σκάνδαλον in Greek, we can say a stumbling-block, or a ruin, or the striking of the foot. Whence: He that shall scandalize anyone, that is, shall have given occasion of ruin.
*Let them alone,* etc. Leave them to their own judgment, because they are past recall. Whence Paul: *A man that is a heretic, after the first and second correction, avoid* ((Tit. III)).
*Expound.* What was said plainly, the apostles think was said in a parable. He is a faulty hearer who wishes to understand either obscure things plainly, or things plainly said obscurely.

*Out of the heart,* etc. For they are not sent in by the devil, but are born of a man's own will. For the devil is an inciter, not an author, since neither does he know inward things save through outward bearing and gesture.

*With unwashen hands.* The spiritual sayings of the prophets, concerning the chastening of the heart and of the body, such as these: *Be washed, be clean ((Isa. I))*. The Pharisees took them carnally, of the body alone, which it is vain to do.

*And going out,* etc. The slanderers being left behind, within the borders of Tyre and Sidon, that he might set the daughter free, and by the faith of a Gentile woman convict the perfidy of the Scribes. "The slanderers being left behind" signifies that after the resurrection he would leave behind the perfidy of the Jews, and would go by his preaching to the Gentiles.

*She cried out,* etc. By faith she cries out, whence, she knows how to call him Son of David, confessing the incarnation of Christ. She prays for her daughter, that is, for her own people not yet believing, that they may be loosed from that very deceit of the devil. Or, the daughter is the soul or the conscience of anyone within the Church that has been made over to the devil, for which mother Church prays, or the man himself for his defiled conscience.

*Who answered not.* Not out of pride, but lest he should be contrary to his own saying: *Into the way of the Gentiles go ye not ((Matth. X))*. Whence he avoids the slander of the Jews, but the salvation of the Gentiles is reserved for the time of the passion and the resurrection.

*I was not sent.* As if he said: First I must fulfil the sacrament of my coming among the Jews, and so bring in other sheep, and this by deferring, in the matter of the sign, the petition of this woman.
*The children's bread.* The word of salvation, which is owed first to the Jews, is not good to give to dogs, or to the Gentiles, that always bark with a dog's madness.

*Yea, Lord.* Under the person of the woman, the marvellous faith of the Church, and her patience, and her humility are proclaimed. Faith, because she believes that her daughter can be healed. Patience, because so often despised she persists in her prayers. Humility, because she compares herself not to dogs, but to whelps.

*For even the whelps.* The table is Holy Scripture; the children's crumbs are the inward mysteries with which the humble are refreshed under the table: because, being humbly subject to the Scriptures, the whelps are the humble Gentiles. The little ones eat not loaves, not crusts, that is, not the surface of the letter, but the marrow.

*Great is the faith.* So above, of the centurion: *I have not found so great faith in Israel ((Matth. VIII))*, who likewise (as this Canaanite woman does) prefigured the faith of the Gentiles. Great is the faith of the Gentiles, who at the hearing of the ear obey: and in God she obtains salvation for herself and for her own. That he heals the centurion's servant and the Canaanite woman's daughter without coming to them signifies that the Gentiles, to whom he did not come by his presence, were to be saved by his word.

*And she was healed.* Here an example is given of catechizing and baptizing infants, who can neither understand nor do anything, but are set free from the devil through the faith and confession of their parents.

O Thou who camest from above

echoes.text: For Yahweh won’t reject his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.
echoes.note: Paul's opening 'God did not reject his people' (v.1-2) verbally tracks the psalm's promise 'the LORD will not reject his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.' Same verb of rejection, same object 'his people'; it functions almost as an embedded near-quotation grounding the whole argument.

echoes.text: For Yahweh will not forsake his people for his great name’s sake, because it has pleased Yahweh to make you a people to himself.
echoes.note: Samuel: 'the LORD will not forsake his people for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself.' Paul's denial of rejection draws on this covenant-fidelity formula; pairs with Ps 94:14 as the scriptural backbone of v.1-2 'God did not reject his people.'

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Verbatim of Elijah's complaint at Horeb: 'they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars; I alone am left, and they seek my life.' Paul cites it formulaically ('don't you know what the Scripture says about Elijah... how he pleads with God against Israel') to introduce the remnant theme (v.3).

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah's complaint is repeated verbatim in 1 Kgs 19:14 (the second utterance to the LORD); Paul's v.3 reproduces this doubled lament. Listed separately because the source occurs at both v.10 and v.14 (recurrence within the source narrative).

echoes.text: Yet will I leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth which has not kissed him.”
echoes.note: Formula-cited divine answer (v.4): 'I have reserved for myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to Baal.' Verbatim of the LORD's reply to Elijah; the foundational proof-text for Paul's doctrine of a preserved remnant 'according to the election of grace' (v.5).

echoes.text: For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers.
echoes.note: Formula-cited ('as it is written') in v.8: 'God gave them a spirit of stupor (pneuma katanyxeos)' is verbatim from Isa 29:10 LXX, 'the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep.' Supplies the head phrase of the conflated citation about Israel's hardening.

echoes.text: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: The continuation of v.8 — 'eyes that they should not see and ears that they should not hear, to this very day' — is verbatim from Deut 29:4 ('the LORD has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day'). Paul fuses it with Isa 29:10 into a single formula-introduced quotation; 'to this very day' is the Deuteronomy tag.

echoes.text: Let their table before them become a snare. May it become a retribution and a trap. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they can’t see. Let their backs be continually bent.
echoes.note: Attributed quotation (v.9-10, 'David says'): 'Let their table be made a snare and a trap... Let their eyes be darkened that they may not see, and bow down their back always.' Verbatim of Ps 69:22-23 LXX. A psalm of the righteous sufferer Paul reads imprecatorily against the hardened; pairs the 'darkened eyes' with the Isaiah/Deut citation of v.8.

echoes.text: For though your people, Israel, are like the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness. For the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will make a full end, and that determined, in the midst of all the earth.
echoes.note: The remnant motif of v.5 ('a remnant according to the election of grace') draws on Isaiah's remnant theology ('though your people be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return'), a text Paul has already quoted in Rom 9:27-28. Strong conceptual borrowing of the 'remnant' (leimma/hypoleimma) word-field.

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: The 'eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear' hardening language of v.8 also resonates with Isaiah's commissioning oracle ('hearing you will hear and not understand; seeing you will see and not perceive'), the classic hardening text. Reinforces the conflated citation's theme even if Deut 29:4 supplies the closer wording.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you. I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
echoes.note: Paul's self-identification as 'a descendant of Abraham' (v.1) leans on the Abrahamic covenant promise to the seed; faint, but it grounds his claim that membership in the people persists by descent and election.

echoes.text: Let destruction come on him unawares. Let his net that he has hidden catch himself. Let him fall into that destruction.
echoes.note: The 'snare/trap' imprecation of v.9 also echoes the wider psalmic curse tradition ('let destruction come upon him unawares, and let his net that he hid catch himself'). Faint reinforcement of the Ps 69 citation.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.
echoes.note: 'My sheep were scattered... they wandered, lost.' Jesus' mission 'to the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Mt 15:24) draws directly on Ezekiel's scattered/lost flock that God himself will seek and shepherd.

echoes.text: My people have been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray; they have turned them away on the mountains; they have gone from mountain to hill; they have forgotten their resting place.
echoes.note: 'My people have been lost sheep; their shepherds have led them astray' — close verbal source for 'the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Mt 15:24).

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]
echoes.note: The Davidic covenant promising an eternal son/throne — basis for the Gentile woman's address 'Lord, you son of David' (Mt 15:22), a messianic title.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: Elijah sent to the Gentile widow of Zarephath, in the region of Sidon, whose son he heals — a typological precedent for Jesus in 'the region of Tyre and Sidon' (15:21) granting mercy and healing to a Gentile woman's child.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray' — the lost/straying sheep image behind 15:24.

echoes.text: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.
echoes.note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' — individual lost-sheep language resonant with Mt 15:24.

echoes.text: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.
echoes.note: 'A shoot from the stump of Jesse' — Davidic-messianic hope behind the 'son of David' acclamation in 15:22.

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,
echoes.note: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn' — Israel's status as God's children illumines 'the children's bread' (Mt 15:26) reserved first for Israel before Gentiles.

echoes.text: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.
echoes.note: 'You are the children of the LORD your God' — Israel as God's children, background to the children-vs-dogs (Israel-vs-Gentiles) contrast of 15:26.

echoes.text: Joshua the son of Nun secretly sent two men out of Shittim as spies, saying, “Go, view the land, including Jericho.” They went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab, and slept there. The king of Jericho was told, “Behold, men of the children of Israel came in here tonight to spy out the land.” The king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, “Bring out the men who have come to you, who have entered into your house; for they have come to […]
echoes.note: Rahab the Canaanite who confesses Israel's God and is saved — a figural precedent for a Canaanite woman whose faith Jesus praises (Mt 15:28); Matthew has already named Rahab in the genealogy.

echoes.text: He said, “Canaan is cursed. He will be a servant of servants to his brothers.” He said, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Shem. Let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth. Let him dwell in the tents of Shem. Let Canaan be his servant.”
echoes.note: The curse on Canaan to be servant — the Canaanite woman's reversal (faith commended) stands against the Canaanite-as-cursed-outsider background flagged by Matthew's pointed label 'a Canaanite woman'.

notes.text: My salvation — That eminent salvation by the Messiah, and in which, without this you shall have no share. Is near - So the scripture often speaks of things which are at a great distance, as if they were present or at hand, Hab. ii, 3 James v, 8, 9 Rev. xxii, 20. My righteousness - The same thing which he called salvation.

Mountain — To my house, which stood upon Mount Zion. Joyful - By accepting their services, and comforting their hearts with the sense of my love. Accepted - They shall have as free access to mine house and altar, as the Jews themselves, and their services shall be as acceptable to me. Evangelical worship is here described under such expressions as agreed to the worship of God which then was in use.
The Lord — Who will gather to himself, and bring into their own land, those that are cast out of their own land. Yet - I will make a far more comprehensive gathering of the Gentiles.

glossa.text:
*Thus saith the Lord. Keep ye judgment.* ((HIER.)) The prophecy of the Gentiles being ended, who at the coming of Christ are changed from nard and nettle into fir and myrtle: he speaks to the hearers of that time, that they may prepare themselves for the coming of the Saviour, who is mercy and justice.

*Keep ye judgment.* ((ID.)) Not accepting the person in judgment. For the judgment is the Lord's, who judges those who judge good things.

*And the children of the stranger:* after the eunuchs he passes to the strangers and promises rewards.

*For servants.* Such as Paul, who says of himself: Paul, the servant of Christ Jesus; and Moses, the servant of God.

*Their holocausts. Mortify your members, which are upon the earth ((Colos. III))*. And *That you present your bodies a victim living unto God .* The holocaust is offered whole to God, and is burnt. A part of the victim is given to the priests. He renders a holocaust to God who leaves the world, that he may always be free for prayer. A victim, he who serves God and disposes justly the things that are of the world.

*Upon my altar.* The faith upon which all things are offered, without which it is impossible to please God. Whence: *But the just man shall live in his faith.*

notes.text: Thy way — The way of truth, or the true religion; the same which in the next clause is called his saving health, and both together signify the way of salvation; deal so graciously with thy people, that thereby the Gentile-world may at last be allured to join with them.
Judge — Rule them. Govern - Hebrew. lead; gently, as a shepherd doth his sheep; and not rule them with rigor, as other lords had done.

Them — When the people of the earth shall be converted to God, God will cause it to yield them abundance of all sorts of fruits. Under which one blessing, all other blessings both temporal and spiritual are comprehended. Our own - He who is Israel's God in a peculiar manner. The occasion of this psalm, seems to have been David's translation of the ark to Zion, which was managed with great solemnity and devotion. For the first words are the very same which Moses appointed for such occasions, Num. x, 35, and the following verses pursue the same matter. Thence he falls into a description of some of the glorious works of the God to whom this ark belonged. But because David knew that both himself and the ark were types of Christ, and that the church of Israel were a type of the catholick church, consisting of Jews and Gentiles, and that the legal administrations were types of those of the gospel, he therefore by the spirit of prophecy, looked through the types, to the great mysteries of Christ's resurrection and ascension, and of the special privileges of the Christian church, and of the conversion of the Gentiles, and intermixes passages, which immediately belong to these things, although the words be so ordered, that they carry a manifest allusion to the present actions, and may be applied to them, in a secondary sense. He first prays against God's enemies, and for his people, ver. 1-3. Then praises God, for his greatness and goodness, ver. 4-6. For his wonderful works, ver. 7-14. For his special presence in his church, ver. 15- 17. The ascension of Christ, and the salvation of his people, ver. 18-20. His victories over his enemies, and favours to his church, ver. 21-28. The accession of the Gentiles to the church, ver. 29- 31. An awful acknowledgment of the glory and grace of God, ver. 32-35. To the chief musician, A psalm or song of David.

glossa.text: *May God have mercy. ((Ibid.))* The blessing of God is first, which is as it were a rain watering the earth of our mind: thence we bless him, which is as it were the fruit; and in both it is we that grow, not he. Let him therefore who desires the rain of the Lord's blessing say: May God have mercy on us, etc. *May God have mercy on us and bless us.* ((CAS.)) But many who wish, etc., *as far as* and because Christ is known among the nations: *Let them confess,* etc. *May he bless us. ((Ibid.))* The Creator blesses the creature, by multiplying it, in number and in merit. The creature blesses the Creator, by praising him with heart, voice and work, and by ascribing to him every good thing that it has.
*Let the peoples confess to thee, O God. ((Ibid.))* After knowledge he exhorts them to confess, for direction and for judgment.
*Let them be glad and rejoice.* ((AUG.)) Because, having now confessed, they do not fear the judgments to come, to whom Christ is an advocate, not a judge, *let them be glad.*

*Let the peoples confess to thee, O God.* ((CAS.)) The same admonition, tending to another thing, because the earth has given her fruit, and although the beginning of the sense is the same, yet it tends to different things.

*The earth hath given her fruit.* ((HIER.)) To Mary, Christ, etc., *as far as:* But not she alone owes this, nay rather, *let him bless* also *us. God, our God. ((Ibid.))* Three times, the Trinity, *him,* the unity. *And let them fear him.* ((CAS.)) Fear is asked for in the midst of benefits, that what is entrusted may be warily kept: the fear of God begins and completes; he who has learned to fear does not cease to love.

notes.text: Hath God rejected his whole people — All Israel? In no wise. Now there is "a remnant" who believe, ver. 5; and hereafter "all Israel will be saved," ver. 26.

God hath not rejected that part of his people whom he foreknew — Speaking after the manner of men. For, in fact, knowing and foreknowing are the same thing with God, who knows or sees all things at once, from everlasting to everlasting. Know ye not - That in a parallel case, amidst a general apostasy, when Elijah thought the whole nation was fallen into idolatry, God "knew" there was "a remnant" of true worshippers.
For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance — God does not repent of his gifts to the Jews, or his calling of the gentiles.

For God hath shut up all together in disobedience — Suffering each in their turn to revolt from him. First, God suffered the gentiles in the early age to revolt, and took the family of Abraham as a peculiar seed to himself. Afterwards he permitted them to fall through unbelief, and took in the believing gentiles. And he did even this to provoke the Jews to jealousy, and so bring them also in the end to faith. This was truly a mystery in the divine conduct, which the apostle adores with such holy astonishment.

glossa.text: *I say then.* Because he had confuted the Jews by so many authorities, the gentiles might insult them, saying that they had been wholly cast off.

*He foreknew.* For *he predestined* he has set *he foreknew*. For so it ought to be taken, as is plain from what follows; and he said *he foreknew* for this reason, lest the Jews should again be proud from that whereby he said that they were not cast off, and were the people of God.

((AUG.)) Or will anyone dare to say that God did not foreknow to whom he was to give that they should believe, or whom he was to give to his Son, that of them he should lose none? And if he foreknew these things, assuredly he foreknew his own benefits, by which he deigns to set us free. This predestination of the saints is nothing else than the foreknowledge, that is, and the preparation, of God's benefits, by which they are most certainly set free, whosoever are set free.

*Or know ye not.* As if he should say: so the Lord has not cast off the remnant in this time, but has saved them; just as in the time of Elias he reserved many to himself, when Elias seemed to himself to be alone; and if he was ignorant that others also besides himself were reserved, it is no wonder if these are ignorant.
*For as.* That is, by what reason God once permitted you not to believe, namely lest you should have cause of being proud after you were converted.
*That they also.* Having learned by experience that salvation is not through the law, but through grace: that so they also may obtain mercy through humility.

*He hath concluded.* That is, he permitted them to be concluded. Here he seems in some manner to expound the mystery. *For God hath concluded all things in the unbelieving,* that they, confounded by repenting of the bitterness of their unbelief, converted by believing to the sweetness of God's mercy, might remain the more humble, so that both the grace of the gift might be most welcome, and they might cry out: *How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord ((Psal. XXX.)) Of all.* That is, of the Jews and of the gentiles, not that he will damn none, which some have falsely supposed.

notes.text: Every plant — That is, every doctrine.
Let them alone — If they are indeed blind leaders of the blind; let them alone: concern not yourselves about them: a plain direction how to behave with regard to all such. Luke vi, 39.
Are ye also yet without understanding — How fair and candid are the sacred historians? Never concealing or excusing their own blemishes.
First evil thoughts — then murders - and the rest. Railings - The Greek word includes all reviling, backbiting, and evil speaking.
Mark vii, 24.

A woman of Canaan — Canaan was also called Syrophenicia, as lying between Syria properly so called, and Phenicia, by the sea side. Cried to him - From afar, Thou Son of David - So she had some knowledge of the promised Messiah.
He answered her not a word — He sometimes tries our faith in like manner.
I am not sent — Not primarily; not yet.
Then came she — Into the house where he now was.
Thy faith — Thy reliance on the power and goodness of God.

glossa.text: *Not that which entereth in.* There is nothing outside a man that defiles him within, nor meat offered to idols in this, that it is God's creature; by one word every superstition of observances is struck down, when religion is thought to lie in distinguishing foods.

*Then the disciples, drawing near.* Great is the Pharisees' religion in the matter of foods, who on hearing this word were scandalized, that is, were indignant. *They were scandalized.* Σκάνδαλον in Greek, we can say a stumbling-block, or a ruin, or the striking of the foot. Whence: He that shall scandalize anyone, that is, shall have given occasion of ruin.
*Let them alone,* etc. Leave them to their own judgment, because they are past recall. Whence Paul: *A man that is a heretic, after the first and second correction, avoid* ((Tit. III)).
*Expound.* What was said plainly, the apostles think was said in a parable. He is a faulty hearer who wishes to understand either obscure things plainly, or things plainly said obscurely.

*Out of the heart,* etc. For they are not sent in by the devil, but are born of a man's own will. For the devil is an inciter, not an author, since neither does he know inward things save through outward bearing and gesture.

*With unwashen hands.* The spiritual sayings of the prophets, concerning the chastening of the heart and of the body, such as these: *Be washed, be clean ((Isa. I))*. The Pharisees took them carnally, of the body alone, which it is vain to do.

*And going out,* etc. The slanderers being left behind, within the borders of Tyre and Sidon, that he might set the daughter free, and by the faith of a Gentile woman convict the perfidy of the Scribes. "The slanderers being left behind" signifies that after the resurrection he would leave behind the perfidy of the Jews, and would go by his preaching to the Gentiles.

*She cried out,* etc. By faith she cries out, whence, she knows how to call him Son of David, confessing the incarnation of Christ. She prays for her daughter, that is, for her own people not yet believing, that they may be loosed from that very deceit of the devil. Or, the daughter is the soul or the conscience of anyone within the Church that has been made over to the devil, for which mother Church prays, or the man himself for his defiled conscience.

*Who answered not.* Not out of pride, but lest he should be contrary to his own saying: *Into the way of the Gentiles go ye not ((Matth. X))*. Whence he avoids the slander of the Jews, but the salvation of the Gentiles is reserved for the time of the passion and the resurrection.

*I was not sent.* As if he said: First I must fulfil the sacrament of my coming among the Jews, and so bring in other sheep, and this by deferring, in the matter of the sign, the petition of this woman.
*The children's bread.* The word of salvation, which is owed first to the Jews, is not good to give to dogs, or to the Gentiles, that always bark with a dog's madness.

*Yea, Lord.* Under the person of the woman, the marvellous faith of the Church, and her patience, and her humility are proclaimed. Faith, because she believes that her daughter can be healed. Patience, because so often despised she persists in her prayers. Humility, because she compares herself not to dogs, but to whelps.

*For even the whelps.* The table is Holy Scripture; the children's crumbs are the inward mysteries with which the humble are refreshed under the table: because, being humbly subject to the Scriptures, the whelps are the humble Gentiles. The little ones eat not loaves, not crusts, that is, not the surface of the letter, but the marrow.

*Great is the faith.* So above, of the centurion: *I have not found so great faith in Israel ((Matth. VIII))*, who likewise (as this Canaanite woman does) prefigured the faith of the Gentiles. Great is the faith of the Gentiles, who at the hearing of the ear obey: and in God she obtains salvation for herself and for her own. That he heals the centurion's servant and the Canaanite woman's daughter without coming to them signifies that the Gentiles, to whom he did not come by his presence, were to be saved by his word.

*And she was healed.* Here an example is given of catechizing and baptizing infants, who can neither understand nor do anything, but are set free from the devil through the faith and confession of their parents.

Who shall stand in God's holy place

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: For Yahweh won’t reject his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.
echoes.note: Paul's opening 'God did not reject his people' (v.1-2) verbally tracks the psalm's promise 'the LORD will not reject his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance.' Same verb of rejection, same object 'his people'; it functions almost as an embedded near-quotation grounding the whole argument.

echoes.text: For Yahweh will not forsake his people for his great name’s sake, because it has pleased Yahweh to make you a people to himself.
echoes.note: Samuel: 'the LORD will not forsake his people for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself.' Paul's denial of rejection draws on this covenant-fidelity formula; pairs with Ps 94:14 as the scriptural backbone of v.1-2 'God did not reject his people.'

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Verbatim of Elijah's complaint at Horeb: 'they have killed your prophets and torn down your altars; I alone am left, and they seek my life.' Paul cites it formulaically ('don't you know what the Scripture says about Elijah... how he pleads with God against Israel') to introduce the remnant theme (v.3).

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah's complaint is repeated verbatim in 1 Kgs 19:14 (the second utterance to the LORD); Paul's v.3 reproduces this doubled lament. Listed separately because the source occurs at both v.10 and v.14 (recurrence within the source narrative).

echoes.text: Yet will I leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth which has not kissed him.”
echoes.note: Formula-cited divine answer (v.4): 'I have reserved for myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to Baal.' Verbatim of the LORD's reply to Elijah; the foundational proof-text for Paul's doctrine of a preserved remnant 'according to the election of grace' (v.5).

echoes.text: For Yahweh has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes, the prophets; and he has covered your heads, the seers.
echoes.note: Formula-cited ('as it is written') in v.8: 'God gave them a spirit of stupor (pneuma katanyxeos)' is verbatim from Isa 29:10 LXX, 'the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep.' Supplies the head phrase of the conflated citation about Israel's hardening.

echoes.text: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: The continuation of v.8 — 'eyes that they should not see and ears that they should not hear, to this very day' — is verbatim from Deut 29:4 ('the LORD has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day'). Paul fuses it with Isa 29:10 into a single formula-introduced quotation; 'to this very day' is the Deuteronomy tag.

echoes.text: Let their table before them become a snare. May it become a retribution and a trap. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they can’t see. Let their backs be continually bent.
echoes.note: Attributed quotation (v.9-10, 'David says'): 'Let their table be made a snare and a trap... Let their eyes be darkened that they may not see, and bow down their back always.' Verbatim of Ps 69:22-23 LXX. A psalm of the righteous sufferer Paul reads imprecatorily against the hardened; pairs the 'darkened eyes' with the Isaiah/Deut citation of v.8.

echoes.text: For though your people, Israel, are like the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. A destruction is determined, overflowing with righteousness. For the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will make a full end, and that determined, in the midst of all the earth.
echoes.note: The remnant motif of v.5 ('a remnant according to the election of grace') draws on Isaiah's remnant theology ('though your people be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return'), a text Paul has already quoted in Rom 9:27-28. Strong conceptual borrowing of the 'remnant' (leimma/hypoleimma) word-field.

echoes.text: He said, “Go, and tell this people, ‘You hear indeed, but don’t understand; and you see indeed, but don’t perceive.’ Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: The 'eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear' hardening language of v.8 also resonates with Isaiah's commissioning oracle ('hearing you will hear and not understand; seeing you will see and not perceive'), the classic hardening text. Reinforces the conflated citation's theme even if Deut 29:4 supplies the closer wording.

echoes.text: I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God to you and to your seed after you. I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
echoes.note: Paul's self-identification as 'a descendant of Abraham' (v.1) leans on the Abrahamic covenant promise to the seed; faint, but it grounds his claim that membership in the people persists by descent and election.

echoes.text: Let destruction come on him unawares. Let his net that he has hidden catch himself. Let him fall into that destruction.
echoes.note: The 'snare/trap' imprecation of v.9 also echoes the wider psalmic curse tradition ('let destruction come upon him unawares, and let his net that he hid catch himself'). Faint reinforcement of the Ps 69 citation.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: They were scattered, because there was no shepherd; and they became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered. My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and on every high hill: yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth; and there was no one who searched or sought.
echoes.note: 'My sheep were scattered... they wandered, lost.' Jesus' mission 'to the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Mt 15:24) draws directly on Ezekiel's scattered/lost flock that God himself will seek and shepherd.

echoes.text: My people have been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray; they have turned them away on the mountains; they have gone from mountain to hill; they have forgotten their resting place.
echoes.note: 'My people have been lost sheep; their shepherds have led them astray' — close verbal source for 'the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Mt 15:24).

echoes.text: When your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever. I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; but my loving kindness shall not […]
echoes.note: The Davidic covenant promising an eternal son/throne — basis for the Gentile woman's address 'Lord, you son of David' (Mt 15:22), a messianic title.

echoes.text: Yahweh’s word came to him, saying, “Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.” So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks: and he called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink.” As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of […]
echoes.note: Elijah sent to the Gentile widow of Zarephath, in the region of Sidon, whose son he heals — a typological precedent for Jesus in 'the region of Tyre and Sidon' (15:21) granting mercy and healing to a Gentile woman's child.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray' — the lost/straying sheep image behind 15:24.

echoes.text: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.
echoes.note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' — individual lost-sheep language resonant with Mt 15:24.

echoes.text: A shoot will come out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots will bear fruit.
echoes.note: 'A shoot from the stump of Jesse' — Davidic-messianic hope behind the 'son of David' acclamation in 15:22.

echoes.text: You shall tell Pharaoh, ‘Thus says Yahweh, Israel is my son, my firstborn,
echoes.note: 'Israel is my son, my firstborn' — Israel's status as God's children illumines 'the children's bread' (Mt 15:26) reserved first for Israel before Gentiles.

echoes.text: You are the children of Yahweh your God. You shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.
echoes.note: 'You are the children of the LORD your God' — Israel as God's children, background to the children-vs-dogs (Israel-vs-Gentiles) contrast of 15:26.

echoes.text: Joshua the son of Nun secretly sent two men out of Shittim as spies, saying, “Go, view the land, including Jericho.” They went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab, and slept there. The king of Jericho was told, “Behold, men of the children of Israel came in here tonight to spy out the land.” The king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, “Bring out the men who have come to you, who have entered into your house; for they have come to […]
echoes.note: Rahab the Canaanite who confesses Israel's God and is saved — a figural precedent for a Canaanite woman whose faith Jesus praises (Mt 15:28); Matthew has already named Rahab in the genealogy.

echoes.text: He said, “Canaan is cursed. He will be a servant of servants to his brothers.” He said, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Shem. Let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth. Let him dwell in the tents of Shem. Let Canaan be his servant.”
echoes.note: The curse on Canaan to be servant — the Canaanite woman's reversal (faith commended) stands against the Canaanite-as-cursed-outsider background flagged by Matthew's pointed label 'a Canaanite woman'.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Joseph wept aloud and told his brothers, I am Joseph.
Do not be distressed; God meant it for good.
How good and pleasant when kindred dwell together.
Mercy has the last word over us.
Even the dogs eat the crumbs from the table, she said.
And great was her faith; the door swung open.
Come, let us worship the God of mercy.
We come to the open table. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture the long table where no one is turned away — even the crumbs that fall from it are enough to heal.
Mercy is wide enough for all.
Joseph could have taken revenge; instead he wept and kissed the brothers who sold him, and forgave.
Mercy is wide enough for all.
A Canaanite woman, an outsider, would not stop asking, and her bold faith opened a door no one expected.
Mercy is wide enough for all.
So whatever name you've worn — outsider, betrayer, the one who came back — there is room and mercy here.
Mercy is wide enough for all. Thanks be to God!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Joseph wept and forgave the brothers who sold him.
Mercy is wide enough for all.
How good when kindred dwell together at last.
Mercy is wide enough for all.
Even the crumbs from the table were enough, she said.
Mercy is wide enough for all.
Come, let us worship the God whose mercy holds us.
Mercy is wide enough for all. Amen.

turn.trap: Becomes either a troubling "test of faith" story that makes Jesus sound cruel on purpose (glossing over how unsettling his silence and the "dogs" line actually are) or gets smoothed into generic "persistence pays off" advice — missing that this is the one story where a Gentile woman changes the shape of Jesus' mission by arguing with him.
turn.hinge: Jesus calls her a dog to her face — and she does not deny it, she uses it. The turn isn't that she out-argues an insult; it's that she takes the insult's own logic and finds mercy already hiding inside it.

doors.landing: She did not deny it, she used it
doors.claim: The woman doesn't dispute being called a dog — she takes the metaphor and finds the mercy already implied inside it: even dogs get crumbs.

witnesses.author: Glossa Ordinaria
witnesses.reading: The great faith of this Chananaean woman is herein shewed. She believes Him to be God, in that she calls Him 'Lord'; and man, in that she calls Him 'Son of David.'

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Wonderful are shewn the faith, patience, and humility of this woman; faith, that she believed that her daughter could be healed; patience, that so many times over...

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: Humility, because she compares herself not to dogs, but to whelps. The little ones eat not loaves, not crusts, that is, not the surface of the letter, but the marrow.

doors.say: She didn't argue that she wasn't a dog — she argued that even dogs get crumbs, and that was enough.
doors.do: Ask them to name a label they've been handed that they could turn into an argument for mercy instead of fighting to remove it.

doors.landing: The delay was not a no
doors.claim: Jesus' silence and hard words are not the final answer — the delay becomes the space where her faith is revealed and honored, not denied.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: This was the cause why Christ was so backward, that He knew what she would say, and would not have her so great excellence hid.

witnesses.author: Glossa Ordinaria
witnesses.reading: If the Lord delays the salvation of a soul at the first tears of the supplicating Church, we ought not to despair, or to cease from our prayers, but rather...

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: He answered her not a word — he sometimes tries our faith in like manner. I am not sent — not primarily; not yet.

doors.say: The silence you're getting right now might not be a no — it might be the room your faith needs to be seen.
doors.do: Have them name a prayer they've stopped praying because the delay felt like rejection, and pray it once more.

doors.landing: Once Israel the son, we the dogs
doors.claim: The categories of "son" and "dog" do not stay fixed — this story is a hinge where insider and outsider trade places.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Wonderful change of things! Once Israel the son, and we the dogs; the change in faith has led to a change in the order of our names.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: When He delivered the Jews from the observance of meats, He then also opened the door to the Gentiles.

doors.say: Whoever you think is permanently on the outside might be one confession away from trading places with you.
doors.do: Ask them to name a category of person they've assumed is permanently "outside," and reconsider it in light of this reversal.

doors.landing: A house of prayer for all peoples
doors.claim: The foreigner is not a guest at the edge of God's house but a worshiper with the same access as anyone born inside it.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: They shall have as free access to mine house and altar, as the Jews themselves, and their services shall be as acceptable to me. Yet — I will make a far more comprehensive gathering of the Gentiles.

doors.say: God doesn't say the foreigner may stand in the back. God says their prayers are just as welcome as yours.
doors.do: Ask them who is treated as a visitor in their church long after they should be family, and to change one thing about how that person is welcomed.

doors.landing: Keep justice, for salvation is near
doors.claim: Isaiah opens with a demand, not a feeling: because God's salvation is near, do justice now, without favoring persons.

witnesses.author: Glossa ordinaria
witnesses.reading: He speaks to the hearers of that time, that they may prepare themselves for the coming of the Saviour, who is mercy and justice. Keep ye judgment: not accepting the person in judgment.

witnesses.author: John Wesley
witnesses.reading: My salvation — that eminent salvation by the Messiah. Is near — so the scripture often speaks of things which are at a great distance, as if they were present or at hand.

doors.say: Salvation is close, Isaiah says, so live like it: judge fairly, and stop playing favorites.
doors.do: Have them name one place they extend grace to people like them and withhold it from people unlike them, and even the scales this week.

complementary.gravity: Isaiah promises that foreigners who hold fast to the covenant will be brought to God's holy mountain, "for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people" (Isaiah 56); the Psalm prays that all the peoples will praise God; Paul says God has shut all up in disobedience that he may have mercy upon all (Romans 11); and a Canaanite mother will not be sent away. The nerve: the circle of God's mercy is wider than the people inside it assumed.

synthesis.convergence: Isaiah opens the temple to the foreigner and the outcast (Isaiah 56); the Psalm asks that every people praise God (Psalm 67); Paul sees mercy headed for all, Jew and Gentile both (Romans 11); and a Canaanite woman, told she is outside, argues her way to the table (Matthew 15). Each reading pushes the walls of God's house outward, and in the Gospel it is the outsider who pushes.
synthesis.claim: God's house was always meant for all peoples, and sometimes it is the outsider at the door who reminds the insiders.
synthesis.here: For a congregation that has quietly settled who belongs, the move is to hear Isaiah's "all people" as a present-tense charge, and to ask who is calling out at their door this week.

semicontinuous.gravity: Joseph, once cast out by his own brothers, reveals himself and weeps: "I am Joseph your brother" (Genesis 45); Paul insists God's gifts and call are irrevocable, that mercy was shown to all so that all might receive mercy (Romans 11); and a Canaanite woman — everything Israel was taught to keep its distance from — out-argues Jesus into healing her daughter. The nerve: mercy keeps finding its way to people standing outside every boundary meant to keep them out.

synthesis.convergence: Joseph, once thrown out, reveals himself to the very brothers who cast him out and weeps over them (Genesis 45); Paul insists God's mercy was always headed toward "all," Jew and Gentile both, because God's gifts are never revoked (Romans 11); and a Canaanite woman — the definition of outsider — receives mercy by refusing to let a boundary be the last word. Every reading names the same reversal: the people furthest outside the family turn out to be exactly who mercy was headed toward.
synthesis.claim: The boundary you assume disqualifies you might be exactly where mercy is waiting to be found.
synthesis.here: For people who assume they're too far outside — too estranged, too late, too other — to qualify for grace, point to the woman who took the very word used to exclude her and found mercy folded inside it.

turn.subtract: Three landings — how she used the insult rather than denying it, the delay as testing (not refusing), or the total reversal of insider/outsider. Choose one and let the others go.
